title: Condon worked with Manhattan Project figures

tellings.quote: he's sometimes credited for helping Oppenheimer pick Los Alamos as the site for the Manhattan Project.
tellings.difference: Where Grusch says only "Condon was involved", Jesse Michels names specific roles: helping Oppenheimer choose Los Alamos and helping draft the McMahon Atomic Energy Act. He also mentions the Los Alamos Primer.
tellings.link_reason: Both tellings are about Edward Condon's part in the 1940s Manhattan Project and atomic-energy work alongside figures like Oppenheimer. The telling gives his roles there in more detail, but it covers the same subject at the same scope.

as_told.title: Condon helps pick Los Alamos and draft McMahon Act

tellings.quote: in fact Conan and Oppenheimer were so close that Condon was partly credited for picking Los Alamos as the focal point for the Manhattan Project
tellings.difference: Adds his Göttingen years with Max Born and the Los Alamos Primer, and says he and Oppenheimer were very close.
tellings.link_reason: Both tell of Condon's Manhattan Project closeness to Oppenheimer and his partial credit for choosing Los Alamos.

as_told.title: Condon's Manhattan Project role and choice of Los Alamos
as_told.place_text: Los Alamos, New Mexico; Göttingen, Germany

tellings.quote: The following notes are based on a set of five lectures given by R. Serber during the first two weeks of April 1943, as an "indoctrination course" in connection with the starting of the Los Alamos Project. The notes were written up by E. U. Condon.

plain: The physicist Edward Condon, the story goes, was in the inner circle of the Manhattan Project, the US wartime programme that built the atomic bomb. David Grusch, a former intelligence official turned whistleblower, says only that "Condon was involved" and links him to Vannevar Bush, the government's wartime science chief. Michels goes further, on his own account. He says Condon was so close to J. Robert Oppenheimer, the physicist who led the bomb laboratory, that he is "partly credited" with choosing Los Alamos, New Mexico, as its site. Michels adds that Condon studied in Göttingen, Germany, under the physicist Max Born and helped draft the McMahon Act, a 1946 atomic energy law. A document backs part of this: the Los Alamos Primer, written at the laboratory in April 1943, says its notes on the physicist Robert Serber's opening lectures "were written up by E. U. Condon." The Primer says nothing about who picked the site.

discussion.text: The Primer records that Condon wrote up Serber's April 1943 lectures at the start of the Los Alamos Project; it says nothing of who chose Los Alamos as the site.
